Between 1936 and 1938 Stalin systematically destroyed his own party, his army officer corps, and millions of ordinary citizens. The peak years of the Great Terror — sometimes called the ‘Yezhovshchina’ — saw roughly 750,000 people shot and over a million sent to forced-labour camps. Why this happened, and how much was Stalin’s personal will, is one of the most contested questions in Soviet history.

The Trigger: the Murder of Kirov

On 1 December 1934, Sergei Kirov, the popular Leningrad party chief, was shot dead at the Smolny Institute by a young dissident, Leonid Nikolaev. Stalin used the murder as proof that hidden enemies were active inside the party. The same day, a decree authorised summary trials and execution of suspected terrorists. Whether Stalin himself ordered the killing remains debated — the totalitarian school argues yes, revisionists say a deranged loner is sufficient. Either way, Kirov’s death triggered the wave of arrests that culminated in the Great Terror.

The Show Trials of the Old Bolsheviks, 1936-1938

Between August 1936 and March 1938, three great Moscow show trials destroyed the surviving leadership of the October Revolution.

  • August 1936 — the ‘Trial of the Sixteen’: Zinoviev, Kamenev and 14 others confessed to plotting with Trotsky to murder Stalin and Kirov. All were shot.
  • January 1937 — the ‘Trial of the Seventeen’: Karl Radek and Yuri Pyatakov among them. Most shot.
  • March 1938 — the ‘Trial of the Twenty-One’: Bukharin, the leading Bolshevik intellectual and former defender of the NEP, confessed and was executed. So was Yagoda, the former NKVD chief.

Confessions were extracted by sleep deprivation, threats to families and prolonged interrogation. The trials were a public theatre: foreign journalists were allowed in to watch defendants admit to fantastic crimes. Western observers split — some accepted the confessions, others (including the philosopher John Dewey’s commission) denounced them as fabrications. Modern historians treat the confessions as forced.

Key Fact

Three Moscow show trials destroyed the Old Bolshevik leadership: the Trial of the Sixteen (Aug 1936, Zinoviev and Kamenev shot), the Trial of the Seventeen (Jan 1937), and the Trial of the Twenty-One (Mar 1938, Bukharin shot). Confessions were extracted by torture and threats to families.

Purge of the Red Army

In June 1937, Marshal Mikhail Tukhachevsky and seven other senior generals were tried in secret and shot, accused of plotting with Nazi Germany. The purge then ran through the officer corps. Of the Red Army’s five marshals, three were shot. Of 80 senior army commanders, 75 were executed or imprisoned. Around 35,000 officers in total — perhaps a third of the corps — were removed. The damage was visible four years later: the early disasters of Operation Barbarossa in 1941 partly reflected an army shorn of its experienced leadership.

The NKVD, Yezhov and the Gulag

The institutional driver was the NKVD (the People’s Commissariat for Internal Affairs), heir to the Cheka. From September 1936 it was led by Nikolai Yezhov — the ‘Yezhovshchina’ takes its name from him. Yezhov set quotas for arrests by region: each NKVD office had a target number of ‘enemies’ to find. Quotas drove denunciations as ordinary Soviets accused colleagues, neighbours and rivals to deflect attention from themselves.

Most arrested were sent to the gulag: a network of forced-labour camps stretching from Solovki to Kolyma in the Soviet Far East. Conditions were brutal — mining gold or felling timber on starvation rations in Arctic temperatures. Estimates of camp deaths in the late 1930s vary; perhaps a million died of cold, hunger and overwork. By 1939 the gulag held around 1.6 million prisoners and was a significant economic asset, building canals, railways and mines.

Yezhov himself was removed from the NKVD in November 1938, arrested the following April, and shot in 1940. Lavrenti Beria replaced him and wound the Terror down somewhat, though arrests and shootings continued. The pattern — Stalin discarding his own enforcers when they became too associated with the violence — would repeat.

The Terror was not limited to old revolutionaries. Mass operations targeted entire categories: ex-kulaks deported in 1929-30, Polish residents of the USSR (around 110,000 shot in the ‘Polish Operation’ of 1937-38), Germans, Latvians and other minorities, plus engineers, priests and teachers. Roughly 750,000 people were executed in 1936-38, with another million-plus sent to camps. Never write that only old Bolsheviks were purged; the mass operations reached far wider.

Censorship, Socialist Realism and the Cult of Personality

A controlled culture sat alongside the violence. Socialist Realism became the only permitted style in 1934: novels, paintings, films and music had to portray heroic workers, wise leaders and a glorious socialist future. Modernist and experimental art was condemned as ‘formalist’. Photographs were retouched to remove disgraced figures — Trotsky was airbrushed out of a famous photograph of Lenin addressing troops in Moscow in 1920; Yezhov was airbrushed out alongside Stalin once he too was purged. School textbooks rewrote the history of the revolution to put Stalin alongside Lenin.

The cult of personality reached its peak. Stalin’s portraits hung in every classroom, factory and kolkhoz. Streets, cities and a tank model bore his name. The 1936 Constitution proclaimed the most democratic political system in the world — a paper document, since real power lay with Stalin and the Politburo. The cult was not just imposed: ordinary Soviets, including many who lost relatives in the Terror, often genuinely believed Stalin was being deceived by NKVD officials acting on their own authority.

Why? The Historiography

Why did the Terror happen? The two main schools clash sharply.

The totalitarian school, led by Robert Conquest in The Great Terror (1968), argues the Purges were driven top-down by Stalin’s personal will to remove rivals and consolidate power. The Terror was deliberate, planned, and centrally directed. Revisionists, led by J. Arch Getty (Origins of the Great Purges, 1985) and Sheila Fitzpatrick, argue the Terror grew partly out of bureaucratic chaos, denunciations from below, and conflict between Moscow and the regions. Stalin set the tone, but quotas and local activists shaped the scale. Both schools agree Stalin was responsible — they disagree on whether the violence was a centrally controlled machine or a chain reaction Stalin lost control of and only later contained. Key Fact

The totalitarian school (Conquest) argues the Terror was driven top-down by Stalin’s personal will. Revisionists (Fitzpatrick, Getty) argue it grew partly from quota culture, denunciations from below and bureaucratic chaos — though Stalin set the political climate that allowed it.
